Years of hosting lavish dinner parties and watching her dishware get chipped during handwashing convinced her the world needed a better way to clean dishes. So, she poured the little money she had left into building a prototype, eventually showcasing her dishwashing contraption at the Chicago World's Fair. This was the first step towards the modern dishwasher, whose basic design remains remarkably similar to Cochrane's. When you press start on a dishwasher, it fills a small basin with water that's heated up to 60°C. Then the pre-wash cycle begins. A circulation pump sends high-pressure water up into spray arms, where it shoots out of angled nozzles, propelling the arms to spin. The water recollects in the basin, where, in most modern models, a turbidity sensor measures the water’s dirtiness by seeing how much light passes through it. The dishwasher then adjusts the wash time and water temperature accordingly and transitions to the wash cycle. Detergent is released and the dishwasher cycles the now-detergent-filled water. This dirty water drains and clean water, heated to an even hotter 68°C, is circulated for a final sanitizing rinse. This is at least 10 degrees warmer than a typical sink’s hottest water, and hot enough to eliminate most foodborne bacteria. Finally, the dishwasher may enter an optional drying cycle. While that's how most dishwashers work, how well they actually clean depends on several factors— the first being the type of detergent you use. Despite their wide-eyed looks, their story is much fiercer than you might imagine. Lorises split off from other primates as far back as 70 million years ago, when T-rexes still roamed. And they gradually migrated from Africa to Asia. Around sunset each evening, lorises get active, moving slowly and deliberately through the trees in their home range. They use their large eyes to scan their surroundings for their next meal and take little time to rest. Pygmy lorises, for one, regularly pass their nights in near-constant motion. Unlike many other primates, however, slow lorises have a higher proportion of slow-twitch muscle fibers, which are favored for long-winded exertion versus speedy spurts. They also have extra vertebrae, making them especially flexible. When needed, slow lorises can stay still, gripped to one tree branch for hours, extra blood vessel networks in their limbs preventing them from weakening or becoming numb. Their slow movements help them go undetected. And that way, they avoid threats, staying stealth around predators that tend to be on the lookout for motion; and they can better hunt unsuspecting prey. Slow lorises are omnivores that go after lots of insects and other small animals, as well as fruit and nectar. Interestingly, they also consume a lot of tree gum and sap, scratching at tree bark with a row of specialized teeth called a “toothcomb.” Though these plant substances are tough to digest, slow lorises seem to be well-equipped to detoxify them.
